title: Cardboard robotic arm
desc: Build a cardboard arm and steer its servos live with potentiometers
content_html:
Materials

  • Arduino Uno & USB cable — 1 (Nerokas, nerokas.co.ke)
  • SG90 micro servo motors — 4 (Nerokas)
  • 10kΩ rotary potentiometers — 4 (Pixel Electronics, pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • Breadboard & jumper wires — 1 set (Nerokas / Pixel Electronics)
  • External 5V power for the servos (4×AA battery holder or 5V supply) — 1 (Pixel Electronics)
  • Corrugated cardboard, a craft knife or scissors, and a hot-glue gun / strong tape
  • A paper fastener (split pin) or short screws for the joints, and a bottle cap for the gripper (optional)

Safety: an adult should do any craft-knife cutting; servos should be powered from the battery/5V supply, not the Arduino's 5V pin, so the board isn't overloaded.

How It Works

A servo motor is a little motor that moves to an exact angle you ask for — anywhere from 0° to 180° — and holds it there. A potentiometer (“pot”) is just a knob: as you turn it, the number the Arduino reads changes from 0 to 1023. The program reads each knob and uses map() to turn that 0–1023 reading into a 0–180 angle, then tells the matching servo to go there. Four knobs steer four servos, so you can drive the whole cardboard arm live with your hands — base, shoulder, elbow and gripper — like a real robot-arm controller.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Build the arm from cardboard first. Cut a sturdy base, then two “bones” for the upper arm and forearm, and two small jaws for the gripper. Keep it light — servos are small.
  2. Fit the servos at the joints. Hot-glue the base servo flat to the base (it spins the whole arm). Glue the shoulder servo where the arm meets the base, the elbow servo between the two bones, and the gripper servo at the end. Attach the white servo horns to the cardboard so each servo moves one joint.
  3. Wire the servos. Each servo has three wires: signal (usually orange/yellow) → Arduino pins 3, 5, 6 and 9; power (red) → the +5V battery/supply rail; ground (brown/black) → the ground rail. Connect the battery ground to the Arduino GND too so they share a common ground.
  4. Wire the potentiometers. For each pot: one outer leg to +5V, the other outer leg to GND, and the middle leg to A0, A1, A2, A3 in turn.
  5. Upload the sketch below and open the arm. Turn each knob — the matching joint should move. Students should watch which knob controls which joint.
  6. Tune and play. If a joint moves the wrong way or hits its limit, reposition the servo horn at a mid-angle and re-glue. Then try picking up a light object with the gripper.

Full Code

#include 

// Four servos make the arm move: base turns left/right, shoulder lifts,
// elbow bends, and the gripper opens/closes.
Servo base, shoulder, elbow, gripper;

// Each servo is steered by its own potentiometer (a knob).
const int POT_BASE = A0, POT_SHOULDER = A1, POT_ELBOW = A2, POT_GRIP = A3;

void setup() {
  // Tell each servo which Arduino pin it is plugged into.
  base.attach(3);
  shoulder.attach(5);
  elbow.attach(6);
  gripper.attach(9);
}

// Read one knob (0–1023) and turn it into a servo angle (0–180 degrees).
int knobToAngle(int pin) {
  return map(analogRead(pin), 0, 1023, 0, 180);
}

void loop() {
  base.write(knobToAngle(POT_BASE));
  shoulder.write(knobToAngle(POT_SHOULDER));
  elbow.write(knobToAngle(POT_ELBOW));
  gripper.write(knobToAngle(POT_GRIP));
  delay(15);   // small pause so the servos move smoothly
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely causeFix
Servos jitter or the Arduino resetsServos powered from the Arduino's 5V — too much currentPower servos from the battery/5V supply and share GND with the Arduino
A joint doesn't move at allSignal wire on the wrong pin, or loose hornCheck the signal wire is on 3/5/6/9 and the horn screw is tight
Joint moves backwardsServo mounted facing the other wayRemount the horn at the opposite side, or swap map() to map(…,0,1023,180,0)
Arm sags or can't liftCardboard too heavy / arm too longShorten the bones and lighten the gripper; keep the load close to the base
Knob does nothingMiddle (wiper) leg not on the analog pin, or outer legs swappedMiddle leg → A0–A3; outer legs → 5V and GND

Discussion Questions

  1. What does the map() function do, and why do we need it between the knob and the servo?
  2. Why must the battery and the Arduino share a common ground?
  3. Real robot arms remember a sequence of moves. How could we make ours repeat a movement automatically?
  4. Which joint has to be the strongest, and why? (Think about which one lifts the most weight.)
  5. Where are robotic arms used in real life, and what jobs do they do better than people?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: add a fifth servo for a wrist twist, or a buzzer that beeps when the gripper closes.
  • Medium: record a move — store a set of angles in the code and add a button that plays them back so the arm repeats a task on its own.
  • Hard: replace the knobs with an app or a second Arduino/joystick so the arm can be controlled wirelessly, or add a light/ultrasonic sensor so it reacts to what's in front of the gripper.
